rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate all six peaks and identify critical pairs while limiting the time penalty. The retention window will guide subsequent gradient trimming and selectivity optimization.
Injection 1 already achieved the maximum CRF of 1.000. Shorten the gradient by one grid step to test a faster separation while retaining full resolution.

The shorter gradient retains maximum CRF but leaves the critical pair close to the resolution threshold. Raise temperature one step to test whether selectivity improves while shortening retention further.

The first temperature increase improved the critical pair and shortened retention while preserving maximum CRF. Test another 5 C increase with the gradient unchanged to assess further gains and monitor the narrowing early pair.
Test the next shorter gradient at 50 C, where all pairs currently have resolution above 2. This will establish whether further compression preserves maximum CRF or makes the middle pair limiting.

Reduce the gradient span to restore a shallower slope between the successful 8-minute and unsuccessful 6-minute runs. The final organic fraction remains well above the estimated last-peak elution fraction, so this should recover full resolution while staying faster than injection 4.

Shift the gradient window upward while preserving the successful slope from injection 6. This should shorten retention; the run will test whether the early and middle pairs retain full resolution at the higher starting organic fraction.

Raise the starting organic fraction to shorten retention, while slightly reducing the slope to protect the marginal middle pair. The final fraction remains above the estimated last-peak elution fraction of about 0.51.

Shift the successful four-minute gradient upward by 0.05 organic fraction, preserving its slope to shorten retention. This tests how far the starting fraction can increase before the early or middle pair loses full resolution.

The middle pair only narrowly missed full resolution in injection 9. Lower the endpoint one grid step to make the gradient shallower and recover maximum CRF, while retaining most of the time savings from the higher starting fraction.

Increase the starting fraction one step while keeping the endpoint fixed, combining earlier elution with a shallower gradient. This tests whether both the early pair and the middle pair remain fully resolved in a faster run.

Maximum CRF is already secured, so test a substantially steeper gradient for a faster alternative. The middle pair may reverse elution order and regain separation beyond its co-elution region; the lower temperature should help preserve early-pair resolution.

Test whether lower temperature improves selectivity for the unresolved middle pair in the fast-gradient regime. Keeping the gradient unchanged isolates the temperature effect, while the short retention window leaves ample room for slower elution.

Test a narrower, higher-starting gradient as an alternative to the poorly resolved steep-gradient regime. Lowering temperature relative to injection 11 may protect early-pair retention and separation, while the shallower slope may help the middle pair.

Return to injection 9, which narrowly missed full resolution, and raise temperature one step to test whether the middle pair recovers while retention shortens. The early pair is the main risk because its resolution decreased with temperature in earlier runs.

With maximum CRF already secured, test a different selectivity regime using a higher starting fraction and low temperature. This may separate the middle pair after an elution-order reversal while preserving enough early retention for a short, fully resolved run.

Test whether a higher starting fraction strengthens separation of the middle pair in the low-temperature regime. Narrowing the gradient span should preserve more separation than simply shifting the entire steep gradient upward, although early-peak compression remains a risk.

Keep the starting fraction and temperature from injection 17, but substantially flatten the gradient to test whether the middle pair reaches full resolution. The lower endpoint may delay the last peak into the hold, but the current retention window leaves ample room below 10 minutes.

The middle pair responded weakly to slope at a 0.40 starting fraction, so test a higher starting fraction to change selectivity. This may improve that pair and shorten the run, though compression of the first two peaks is now the main risk.

Use the lower starting fraction to recover early-pair separation, with a modest temperature increase to test middle-pair selectivity in this high-organic regime. The intermediate endpoint balances the retention time and resolution seen in injections 17 and 18.
Return to the established fully resolved region and test a slope between injections 9 and 10. This should recover the middle pair’s full credit while eluting the last peak sooner than injection 10.

Slightly increase the slope relative to injection 11, the fastest fully resolved method so far, while keeping its starting fraction and temperature. This tests whether its small middle-pair resolution margin permits further shortening of retention.

The steeper variant lost full resolution, so reduce the slope below injection 11 to build a safer middle-pair margin. This tests a more robust maximum-CRF method while keeping retention comfortably below 10 minutes.

Lower temperature one step from injection 23 to improve the limiting early pair, using the middle pair’s resolution margin to accommodate the selectivity shift. This tests a more balanced, fully resolved method while remaining well below the time-penalty threshold.

Increase the endpoint one step from injection 24 to shorten retention while using its middle-pair resolution margin. This also tests whether the fastest fully resolved method, injection 11, retains maximum CRF at a 5 C lower temperature.
